summary.text: Optics is the study of light, and the technology built to manipulate it, from lenses and mirrors to lasers and fibre optics.
Practical optics usually uses simplified models: geometric optics treats light as straight rays that bend or reflect, and physical optics adds wave effects like diffraction and interference.
Light is understood as electromagnetic radiation, and effects that need both wave and particle behavior call for quantum mechanics and photons.

facts.label: Word origin
facts.value: From a Greek word meaning 'appearance' or 'look'

facts.label: Earliest lenses
facts.value: Polished crystal lenses from Crete, as early as 2000 BC

facts.label: Model order
facts.value: The ray model came first, then the wave model

facts.label: Fields that use it
facts.value: Astronomy, photography, medicine and many engineering fields

items.prompt: You want to work out where a mirror will send a beam of light. Which simple model suits the job?

options.label: Geometric optics, with light as straight rays that reflect
Quantum optics, with every photon tracked one by one
A full wave model that ignores rays altogether
Ancient models that hold light is made of water

items.explain: Geometric optics treats light as rays that travel in straight lines and bend or reflect at surfaces, which is the usual practical tool.

items.prompt: Light passing through a narrow gap fans out and forms bands of bright and dark. Why can't the ray model explain this?

options.label: Rays can only describe light that is moving very slowly
Rays cannot bend when they hit any surface at all
Rays only work for mirrors and never for lenses
Diffraction and interference are wave effects that rays miss

items.explain: Physical optics includes wave effects such as diffraction and interference, which geometric optics cannot account for.

items.prompt: In what order did people develop models of light?

options.label: The wave model first, then rays, then electromagnetic radiation
Rays first, then waves, then electromagnetic waves in the 19th century
Photons first, then rays, then waves
All three models arrived together in ancient Greece

items.explain: The ray model came first, followed by the wave model; 19th-century progress showed light waves are electromagnetic radiation.

items.prompt: Some experiments need light to act as both a wave and a particle. What does explaining them require?

options.label: Mirrors with a more rotationally symmetric shape
Better lenses made from polished crystal
Quantum mechanics, with light modelled as photons
Simply measuring the rays more carefully

items.explain: Phenomena that depend on both wave-like and particle-like properties need quantum mechanics, which models light as photons.

items.prompt: A doctor uses a CT scan and an astronomer uses a telescope. What does this show about optical science?

options.label: It is limited to the design of eyeglasses
It is studied only within pure physics
It matters only for lasers and fibre optics
It is relevant across fields like medicine and astronomy

items.explain: Optical science is studied in many disciplines, including astronomy, engineering, photography and medicine.

items.prompt: Why do practical optics designers often use simplified models instead of a complete electromagnetic description?

options.label: The full description is often difficult to apply in practice
The full description has been shown to be incorrect
Light has no electromagnetic nature to describe
Simplified models are always more accurate

items.explain: Most optical phenomena fit classical electromagnetic theory, but complete descriptions are often hard to use, so simplified models are common.
